strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: systematic evaluation of T2I models on long, detail-rich prompts (avg. 284.89 tokens), well beyond the ~100-token limits of prior long-prompt benchmarks (DPG-Bench, DensePrompts).

The data construction pipeline is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: it combines MLLM extraction with auxiliary grounding tools (open-set detector YOLOE, BLIP matching, IoU-based bounding box validation, cropping/highlighting) rather than relying purely on end-to-end LLM generation, which helps reduce hallucination in the annotations.

Extensive robustness analysis beyond what is typical: cross-evaluator consistency check with an independent MLLM (InternVL3-9B, Kendall's tau ~0.88-1.0), random-seed variance analysis (<0.5% deviation), a resource-efficient mini-benchmark that preserves ranking trends, and demonstrated compatibility with external quality/safety metrics.

Evaluation covers a wide and relevant set of 12 models (7 general-purpose incl. proprietary GPT Image-1/Gemini, 5 long-prompt-specialized), yielding interpretable, actionable insights (e.g., long-prompt training matters more than context window size; decomposition/iterative refinement helps; scene attributes are easiest while spatial reasoning is hardest).

Human expert evaluation of benchmark data quality is reported in detail across sub-tasks (Table 5-8), and case studies with qualitative failure analysis (Appendix M, P) add useful color to the quantitative findings.
The negative correlation between prompt length and both character omission and attribute-binding accuracy (isolated by only scoring present characters) is a nice, non-trivial empirical finding.
weaknesses: Potential residual circularity: although the authors argue auxiliary tools mitigate self-enhancement bias, both the 'ground-truth' attribute annotations and the evaluation judgments are ultimately produced by MLLMs (Qwen family primarily, cross-checked with only one alternative model). Their own human evaluation shows ~88-91% image-alignment for some categories (e.g., entity relationships, person attributes, lighting), meaning a non-trivial fraction of the 'ground truth' used for scoring may itself be inaccurate or hallucinated — this is a validity concern for the metric itself, not just the dataset.

Human evaluation was conducted only on the benchmark construction/annotation quality (400 samples), not on the actual image-generation evaluation stage (i.e., no human verification that the automated MLLM judgments of generated images match human judgments of attribute presence/location/relationship correctness). This leaves the core scoring pipeline's fidelity less directly validated than the dataset itself.

The prompts are LLM-rewritten/expanded versions of original captions with attributes explicitly inserted; it is unclear whether these read as natural 'long prompts' a real user would write, or as artificially exhaustive enumerations, which could systematically disadvantage models not trained on such stylistically distinct text (a construct-validity concern for the benchmark's ecological validity).

No new method or mitigation is proposed beyond hypothesized future directions (structure-aware encoders, object-centric diffusion) — appropriate for a benchmark paper, but it limits the technical contribution to dataset/protocol engineering plus empirical analysis.

Comparisons between long-prompt-optimized models and general-purpose SOTA models are somewhat unfair since the optimized methods are built on outdated backbones (SD1.5/SD-XL); the paper acknowledges this but it complicates some of the causal claims about what drives long-prompt adherence (training vs. backbone capacity are confounded).

The spatial partitioning scheme (nine overlapping regions) and its 75% coverage threshold, while validated via one MLLM's binary judgment (95%+ 'accuracy'), is a coarse notion of 'correct location' that may not capture more nuanced positional relationships in complex scenes.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing T2I benchmarks (T2I-CompBench, HRS-Bench, DPG-Bench, DensePrompts) use much shorter prompts (12-100 tokens on average) than the 284.89-token prompts introduced here, and the benchmark decomposes evaluation into four interpretable dimensions (character attributes, locations, scene attributes, relationships) rather than a single alignment score.

Scale and annotation density are substantial (4,116 prompts, 37,165 character attributes, 18,526 relationship annotations), and the data construction pipeline is reasonably well documented with concrete extraction/validation steps (bounding-box voting via IoU + BLIP, attribute filtering, etc.).

The authors conduct an unusually extensive set of robustness checks in the appendix: cross-MLLM re-evaluation (InternVL3-9B) with Kendall's Tau correlation, random-seed stability analysis, human evaluation of data quality, a mini-benchmark, and compatibility checks with external metrics (ImageReward, HPSv2.1, etc.).

The empirical findings (progressive degradation with prompt length, difficulty hierarchy across sub-tasks, attribute leakage isolated from character omission) are presented with supporting quantitative breakdowns (Table 3, Figure 3, Appendix M/N) rather than only qualitative claims.
12 models spanning open-source, proprietary, and long-prompt-specialized categories are evaluated, giving a reasonably broad comparative picture.
weaknesses: Fundamental circularity in the pipeline: the same LLM/MLLM family (Qwen2.5) is used to (a) decide which attributes exist in the source caption/image, (b) rewrite the prompt to include them, and (c) later judge (via a still LLM-based evaluator) whether the generated image contains them. Even though InternVL3-9B is used for a secondary check, that check only confirms rank correlation, not that the underlying "ground-truth" attribute set itself is accurate/unbiased -- the benchmark's notion of "correct generation" is defined by what one LLM believed was in the image, which is a weaker form of ground truth than human-defined ground truth annotations typical of established benchmarks.

The 'long prompts' are synthetically inflated via multi-stage LLM rewriting/expansion of existing short captions rather than naturally occurring detail-rich prompts from real professional use cases (the paper's own motivating scenarios: interactive media, industrial prototyping, visual storytelling). It is unclear whether the resulting prompts reflect realistic long-prompt phrasing/structure that a professional user would actually write, or whether they contain LLM-typical redundancy/awkward phrasing that itself confounds model performance.

Human evaluation supporting benchmark quality is thin relative to the dataset size: only 50 samples per task (400 of 4,116, ~10%) rated by 2 annotators, with no inter-annotator agreement reported, and the criteria (task relevance, image fidelity, prompt consistency) do not assess prompt naturalness/fluency or whether a real user would produce such a prompt.

The core evaluation metric is essentially binary MLLM-as-judge for every fine-grained attribute/relationship/location, a method the paper itself criticizes competitor benchmarks for using in a coarser form; the paper's own hardest metric (Character Locations) is exactly the type of spatial reasoning MLLMs are known to struggle with, raising the concern that some 'model failures' may partly be evaluator failures rather than purely generator failures.

The long-prompt-optimized baselines (LLM4GEN, ELLA, LongAlign, LLM Blueprint, ParaDiffusion) are all built on outdated SD1.5/SDXL backbones from 2023-2024; no long-prompt-specific method is evaluated on a modern flow-matching backbone (e.g., FLUX, SD3.5), which weakens the generalizability of the paper's central claim that 'training matters more than context window' since backbone confounds are not disentangled.

Several of the paper's headline conclusions (long-prompt training helps more than raw context length; decomposition/iterative refinement mitigates errors; performance degrades with prompt length; SOTA models still fail on fine-grained compositional binding) are directionally unsurprising given prior literature on compositional T2I generation and CLIP token limits, somewhat limiting the novelty of the insights beyond the dataset/benchmark artifact itself.

The evaluation pipeline is computationally expensive (~10 hours/model on a single L20 GPU, 20-39GB VRAM), and while a mini-benchmark is offered, the full protocol's reliance on repeated MLLM calls for every attribute may limit adoption and reproducibility by the broader community despite claimed open-sourcing.

The post-hoc explanation for the 'style degradation' finding (attributing it to the benchmark's own bias toward realistic styles) suggests a benchmark construction artifact that could also affect other dimensions but is not systematically investigated.

strengths: Addresses a clear and underexplored gap: existing T2I benchmarks focus on short prompts, while DetailMaster provides long (avg 284.89 tokens), detail-rich prompts with four well-motivated evaluation dimensions (Character Attributes, Character Locations, Scene Attributes, Entity Relationships).

Data construction pipeline is thorough and grounded rather than purely LLM-generated: it uses open-set object detectors, BLIP-based box verification, image cropping/highlighting, and human-annotated source captions to reduce hallucination and self-referential bias.

Extensive robustness analyses are provided, including cross-MLLM-evaluator consistency (InternVL3-9B vs Qwen), random-seed stability, human evaluation of annotation quality (near 90-100% across sub-metrics), and a mini-benchmark that preserves ranking trends — this substantially strengthens confidence in the benchmark's reliability and reproducibility.

Broad and relevant model coverage (7 general-purpose + 5 long-prompt-optimized models, including proprietary SOTA systems), yielding actionable insights (e.g., token capacity vs. long-prompt training, decomposition/iteration strategies, attribute leakage, negative correlation between prompt length and accuracy).
Good transparency about limitations (Appendix O) and detailed appendices covering evaluation protocol, prompt design, and case studies, aiding reproducibility.
Open-sourcing of dataset, code, and evaluation tools (including Data-Juicer integration) supports community adoption and future research.
weaknesses: Evaluation metrics rely entirely on MLLM binary judgments (yes/no) for attribute/location/relationship correctness; despite robustness checks, this is still a proxy measure and may not capture partial correctness, ambiguous cases, or subtle attribute leakage as reliably as claimed.

The benchmark's prompts are synthetically 'polished' via LLM expansion of original captions rather than naturally occurring long prompts, which may introduce stylistic artifacts (verbose, templated phrasing) not fully representative of how practitioners write long prompts in professional applications.

Long-prompt optimized baselines are mostly built on outdated backbones (SD1.5/SD-XL) due to unavailability of newer open-source variants, limiting the paper's ability to disentangle 'long-prompt training' benefits from backbone capacity — the paper acknowledges but cannot fully resolve this confound.

The character localization scheme (9-region partitioning with overlaps) and evaluation thresholds (e.g., 75% bbox coverage, IoU 0.7) involve several manually tuned design choices whose sensitivity is not extensively ablated beyond a single comparison.

Explanatory claims about root causes ('text encoders flatten compositional grammar', 'diffusion models suffer attribute leakage') are stated as hypotheses without direct mechanistic/causal validation, which is honestly flagged but somewhat weakens the depth of the paper's diagnostic contribution.

Some presentation redundancy (e.g., repeated GPT-4 references in bibliography, dense appendix) and the main paper's core insights depend heavily on appendix material for full support of robustness claims.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing T2I benchmarks predominantly use short prompts (10-100 tokens), while this work introduces prompts averaging 284.89 tokens that better reflect professional/detailed use cases, with clear taxonomy across four evaluation dimensions (Character Attributes, Locations, Scene Attributes, Entity Relationships).

Exceptionally thorough empirical validation and robustness analysis: the appendix includes cross-evaluator consistency checks (Qwen2.5-VL vs InternVL3), randomness/seed analysis, small-evaluator feasibility studies, human evaluation across all four task categories, and explicit checks for self-enhancement bias when evaluating family-matched encoder models (e.g., Qwen-Image). This level of rigor is uncommon in benchmark papers and substantially strengthens the reliability of the reported conclusions.

Broad and diverse evaluation covering 19+ models spanning five distinct paradigms (classical diffusion, long-prompt-optimized, LLM/MLLM-encoder models, autoregressive/unified models, and proprietary SOTA), yielding a genuinely informative difficulty hierarchy (Character Locations > Person Attributes > Entity Relationships > Scene Attributes) that is corroborated across multiple additional model families in the appendix.

The controlled 2x2 ablation study (token limit x training prompt length) is a valuable and clean experimental design that isolates a specific, non-obvious insight (long-prompt training matters more than expanded context length alone, but the two factors are synergistic) and additionally validates that gains transfer to short-prompt benchmarks (T2I-CompBench), enhancing the practical significance of the finding.

Data construction pipeline is well-engineered with multiple grounding techniques (open-set detection, BLIP matching, image cropping, MLLM verification) that appear to meaningfully mitigate pure LLM-hallucination risk, and the reported human-evaluation metrics (task relevance, image alignment, prompt consistency) are largely near-ceiling, supporting the claimed data quality.

Practical contributions such as a mini-benchmark (800 prompts) and a lightweight small-evaluator option lower the barrier to adoption, and demonstrated compatibility with external metrics (ImageReward, Aesthetic, HPS, NSFW detectors) broadens the benchmark's usability.
weaknesses: Reliance on MLLM-based binary judgments (yes/no) for fine-grained attribute, location, and relationship verification is inherently coarse and could obscure partial correctness or ambiguous cases; although robustness across evaluators is checked, the underlying evaluation paradigm (single MLLM judge per instance) remains a potential source of systematic bias not fully eliminated by the cross-evaluator experiments, which only confirm rank consistency, not absolute accuracy validity.

The prompts are synthetically expanded via a multi-stage LLM/MLLM pipeline from original captions, which, despite being grounded in real images, produces highly structured, exhaustively itemized prose (as seen in the qualitative examples) that may not fully represent naturalistic professional prompts; the claim of being a 'proxy for professional-grade prompt adherence' is asserted rather than empirically validated against actual professional prompt corpora.

The central mechanistic explanations offered (failure due to weak encoders' inability to parse syntactic dependencies, and 'attribute leakage' in diffusion models) are largely inferred post-hoc from aggregate accuracy patterns and qualitative case studies rather than being directly probed via targeted diagnostic experiments (e.g., attention analysis, controlled syntactic perturbation tests), somewhat limiting the causal strength of these claims.

The key ablation study demonstrating that long-prompt training outperforms mere context-window expansion is conducted on a single modified SD-XL/T5 architecture with a specific semantic-connector design; while informative, generalization of this exact quantitative finding to other architectures (e.g., transformer-based diffusion backbones, autoregressive models) is not independently verified within the ablation itself.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully address relevant considerations such as licensing/copyright status of source images (DOCCI, Flickr30k, COCO subsets) repurposed and augmented via LLMs for a new public benchmark, or potential downstream biases introduced by the LLM-driven attribute extraction and augmentation pipeline (e.g., stereotyped attribute associations for 'person' category).

Given the extraordinarily large appendix (over 20 subsections) relative to a fairly conventional main paper structure, a nontrivial share of the paper's novel analytical content and even some core validation (e.g., human evaluation details, several robustness checks) is relegated to supplementary material, which could affect self-containedness of the main submission.

strengths: Large-scale, carefully constructed benchmark (4,116 prompts, avg. 284.89 tokens) that is substantially longer and more detail-dense than prior long-prompt T2I benchmarks (DPG-Bench, DensePrompts, OneIG-Bench), addressing a genuine and underexplored gap in T2I evaluation.

Comprehensive evaluation covering 19 models across five distinct paradigms (classical diffusion, long-prompt-optimized, LLM/MLLM-encoder, autoregressive/unified, proprietary SOTA), giving a broad and up-to-date picture of the field.

Extensive robustness analysis in the appendix: cross-evaluator consistency checks (Qwen-VL vs InternVL3-9B, Kendall's Tau up to ~0.97), randomness/seed analysis, lightweight-evaluator validation, and human evaluation of annotation quality — these collectively support that the benchmark's relative model rankings are reasonably stable.

The controlled 2x2 ablation study (token limit x training prompt length) isolates a genuinely useful insight: architectural capacity alone is insufficient, and explicit long-prompt training is the primary driver of gains, with synergy between the two factors.

Fine-grained taxonomy (Character Attributes, Locations, Scene Attributes, Entity Relationships) and per-category breakdown (object/animal/person) enable diagnostic analysis beyond coarse CLIPScore-style metrics, revealing a clear difficulty hierarchy and phenomena such as attribute leakage under prompt-length growth.
weaknesses: The evaluation metric is fundamentally an MLLM-as-judge binary VQA scheme; the paper's own experiments show absolute scores swing by 15-20+ points when switching evaluators (Qwen2.5-VL-7B vs InternVL3-9B), indicating that the reported accuracy numbers are not reliable in an absolute sense and only rank-order comparisons are defensible — this significantly undercuts claims like "even SOTA models plateau around 50%" as objective facts rather than artifacts of the chosen judge.

The data construction and evaluation pipelines both rely heavily on LLMs/MLLMs (primarily Qwen family) for attribute extraction, filtering, and verification; while the paper argues this is mitigated by auxiliary grounding tools, the core judgments (e.g., "is this attribute present") remain LLM opinions, so systematic biases of the underlying model family could still propagate through both data and evaluation despite the cross-family checks provided.

The "Character Location" metric relies on a coarse 9-region spatial partitioning scheme (each region covering large, overlapping portions of the image); this coarseness may partly explain why this dimension is reported as the "hardest" and could be conflating genuine model failure with an imprecise/loose ground-truth definition of correct placement.

Methodological novelty is limited: the pipeline largely combines existing off-the-shelf components (MLLM extraction, YOLOE open-set detection, BLIP matching, LLM filtering) in a fairly standard multi-stage recipe; the primary contribution is scale and detail density rather than new evaluation methodology or new modeling insight.

The final prompts are LLM-synthesized expansions that integrate extracted attributes into the original caption, rather than naturally-occurring long prompts from professional users; despite being "grounded" in real images, the resulting prompt style (dense enumeration of separately-extracted attributes) may not faithfully represent how real detailed prompts are written, which could limit the benchmark's ecological validity for the stated goal of representing "professional-grade" prompts.

The key ablation study demonstrating that "long-prompt training matters more than token capacity" is conducted on a single custom SD-XL variant with a lightweight trainable connector; generalization of this specific finding to other architectures (e.g., DiT-based flow models, autoregressive/unified models) is not directly verified.

The "attribute leakage" narrative used throughout the paper to explain failures is inferred post-hoc from length-vs-accuracy correlations rather than measured with a dedicated, targeted leakage metric (e.g., explicitly checking whether an attribute is incorrectly bound to a different entity), so the mechanistic explanation remains somewhat speculative.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not engage with content-specific ethical considerations relevant to this benchmark, such as the use of real images/captions containing people and their described attributes, or potential demographic biases embedded in the extracted "Person Attributes."

strengths: Addresses a clear and underserved gap: existing T2I benchmarks are dominated by short prompts (COCO ~10.5 tokens, CC12M ~20.2 tokens), while DetailMaster provides prompts averaging 284.89 tokens with structured, expert-validated annotations across four compositional dimensions (Character Attributes, Character Locations, Scene Attributes, Entity Relationships).

The data construction pipeline is unusually thorough: it grounds LLM/MLLM outputs with auxiliary tools (open-set detection, BLIP scoring, cropping/highlighting, a custom spatial partitioning scheme empirically shown to reduce boundary ambiguity from 66% to 33% 'null' labels while preserving ~95% positional accuracy), and includes multiple explicit filtering/verification stages to reduce hallucinated attributes.

Extensive robustness analyses are provided beyond the main text: cross-evaluator consistency (Qwen2.5-VL vs. InternVL3-9B, Kendall's Tau up to ~0.97-1.0), lightweight-evaluator validation (3B model preserving rankings), random-seed stability (Δ<0.5%), and an explicit self-enhancement bias check for family-matched encoder/evaluator pairs (Qwen-Image). This substantially strengthens confidence that the benchmark measures genuine model capability rather than evaluator artifacts.

The evaluation spans 19 models across five distinct paradigms (classical diffusion, long-prompt-optimized, LLM/MLLM-encoder models, autoregressive/unified models, proprietary SOTA), offering a broad and current empirical picture, and is further extended in the appendix to very recent systems (Qwen-Image, BAGEL, Nano Banana 2).

The controlled 2x2 ablation study (token limit x training prompt length) isolates and disentangles two conflated factors and yields a clear, well-supported takeaway (long-prompt training matters more than extended context alone, with the two factors being synergistic), which is a genuinely useful mechanistic insight for the field.

Detailed error analysis (statistical hardness hierarchy, qualitative failure categorization, attribute leakage analysis isolating misalignment from omission) provides actionable diagnostic value beyond a single aggregate score.

Human evaluation of the benchmark data itself is reasonably comprehensive (400 samples, multiple criteria per task) and quantifies the information deficit in source captions (e.g., 93.26% missing location information), justifying the need for the augmentation pipeline.
weaknesses: The evaluation pipeline itself (binary yes/no MLLM judgments of generated images against attributes/locations/relationships) is not independently human-validated at scale against actual generated images; the human evaluation in the main text/Appendix G validates the source annotations and prompts, not the downstream scoring judgments on generated outputs, leaving a gap in end-to-end reliability evidence despite the cross-evaluator consistency checks.

The data construction and initial evaluation both rely primarily on the Qwen model family; although the paper provides a self-enhancement bias check and cross-evaluator agreement, this is a single targeted experiment (one model, Qwen-Image) rather than a systematic study, and residual concerns about shared inductive biases between data-generation and evaluation models are only partially addressed.

The core ablation study demonstrating 'long-prompt training matters more than token capacity' is conducted on a single modified SD-XL architecture with a frozen backbone and only a trainable semantic connector; generalizability of this conclusion to other architectures (e.g., DiT-based or autoregressive models) is asserted but not directly tested.

The claim that DetailMaster prompts serve as a 'proxy for professional-grade prompt adherence' is not empirically validated against real professional/industrial prompt distributions; the prompts are synthetically expanded captions from DOCCI/Localized Narratives via LLM augmentation, and their representativeness of genuine professional use cases remains an assumption.

The paper's narrative around causal mechanisms (e.g., 'weak encoders fail to preserve syntactic dependencies,' 'diffusion models suffer from attribute leakage') is largely inferred post-hoc from aggregate correlations and qualitative case studies rather than isolated via targeted causal experiments, so these explanations, while plausible, are not rigorously established.

The extensive appendix (23 lettered sections) means several important robustness and validity arguments (e.g., evaluator randomness, small-model evaluator validity, bias mitigation) are relegated outside the main paper, making the core submission somewhat dependent on supplementary material for its central validity claims.

The Impact Statement is minimal and does not engage with relevant considerations such as reliance on proprietary APIs, potential licensing/attribution issues from derivative use of captioning datasets, or computational costs of the pipeline (which the paper itself reports as substantial, e.g., 55-77 GPU-hours per stage).
